name: Accountability for AI Written Submissions
blurb: Who is responsible when AI drafts regulatory content.
title: Accountability for AI Written Submissions
answer: No regulator has a separate route for AI authored content. Sponsors remain fully accountable for submissions, and where AI produces data supporting a regulatory decision, the FDA expects evidence of the model's credibility for that use.

reading.body:
Accountability for an AI written submission stays with the sponsor, not the tool. No regulator has created a separate route for AI authored content.

The FDA's position is that where a model produces data supporting a regulatory decision, the sponsor must show the model is credible for that specific use. That is a higher bar than disclosure. It means the evidence for the model's fitness travels with the submission, and a named author and reviewer must sit behind every section regardless of what drafted it.

This matters for AI scaling in a narrow way. Regulatory writing is one of the few enterprise tasks where the output is judged by an external body with the power to reject it, so the cost of an unverified draft is not rework but delay. The credibility requirement pushes work back onto people who can defend a model's output, which caps how much of the drafting pipeline can be automated without a matching investment in validation.

The data covers one proposed FDA framework from January 2025 and the general principle that sponsors remain accountable. It does not say what the framework requires in detail, whether it was finalised, how other regulators treat the same question, or how credibility is demonstrated in practice.

sections.body: Keep a named author and reviewer for every section, whatever drafted it.
